title: Most Zugzwang ever Zugzwanged
reviewNotes: Three branches, 17 exact positions from the complete six-piece root. Be6 ...Rb3 Bd6 ...Rc3+ Kd2 ...Rxf3 Ke2 preserves the source’s intervening king move and pawn capture. ...Rf6 Be5+ forks the rook with check; ...Rc3 Be5 pins it, followed by ...Kb2 Kd2. Bg8 ...Rb3 Bxb3 is actual stalemate. Source advertising overlay is omitted.
transcript: The chosen one finds himself in a pretty complicated position, but he's the chosen one for a reason, and he knows how to outplay the evil villain with his bishops. The immediate issue is that this bishop is under attack by the black king. And if white is not careful about where it moves this bishop, black is actually going to be able to pin it to the king and then win it. And now this is simply a draw. And for example, bringing the bishop all the way to G8 allows the brilliant counter punch by black with a rook to B3. A full rook sacrifice that cannot be accepted by the chosen one because if the rook is taken, [music] this is a stalemate. But unfortunately, this move also forks the bishop and the pawn. But white has a secret resource with bishop to D6. And now, of course, if black naively takes the pawn, this is simply a checkmate with the two bishops and king. But unfortunately, the villain can play rook to C3 check, force the king to move, and only then pick up the pawn. And now the rook against the two bishops will be enough to save the draw. So, it's not very clear what white is supposed to do with this light square bishop. But the chosen one knows what to do. And he goes bishop to E6. Now, the idea is not very clear. Black can still play the brilliant rook to B3. And he is still forking these two pieces, but white fearlessly plays bishop to D6. It seems like black can simply throw in this check again, make the king move, and then pick up the pawn. But this is where white uncquirs a majestic move with king to E2. Of course, this rook is under attack, but black has so many squares to move to, right? Well, not exactly. Look at these bishops. They're defending here and here, here and here, here and here. The king is defending these four squares right here. And so the only two squares available to the rook are either this one or this one. But you might notice something. Both of those squares are on this diagonal. Meaning that once the rook moves to this one, there is going to be a fork between the king and rook and if the rook moves to this one, there is going to be a pin. And even if the king tries to defend the rook now, king to D2 adds more pressure to the rook. And no matter what black does on the next move, he's going to lose the rook and the game.
